title: The Village Without Water
summary: When a small village's water tank runs dangerously low during a drought, the council and the village's children work together to ration water fairly and uncover a forgotten backup source.
poll: One person's small effort cannot make a real difference during a big problem like a drought.

versions.title: The Village Without Water
versions.text:
It did not rain. Weeks went by. The village was hot and dry. Everyone felt it.

Lama looked at the big tank. It holds water for the village. The water was low. She felt scared.

Lama told her dad. Dad told the council. A council helps run the town. They made a plan. Each home got two buckets a day. This plan is a ration.

Grandpa had an idea. Long ago, there was a cistern. It is an old hole for rain. It sat by the mosque. Weeds hid it well.

Kids and dads dug it out. The water was still good! Now there were two spots for water.

At last, a big truck came. It filled the tank. The village was safe. People learned to share.

It had not rained for weeks. The village of Zahra was hot and dry.

One morning, Lama looked at the tank. It holds water for the village. She saw the water was low. This worried her.

Lama ran to tell her dad. He told the village council. A council is a group of people. They help run the village. The council made a plan. Each family got two buckets a day. This plan is called a ration.

That night, Grandpa had an idea. Long ago, people used an old cistern. A cistern is a stone hole. It holds rain water. It was behind the mosque. Dust and weeds hid it.

The next day, Lama and her friends helped dig it out. The water was still clean. Now there were two spots for water.

At the end of the week, a truck came. It filled the tank. The village was safe. Everyone learned to share water.

It had not rained in Zahra for many weeks. The ground had become hard and dry. Everyone felt that something was wrong.

One hot morning, Lama climbed the hill. She went to check the big water tank. The tank stores water for every family. She was surprised. The water had become very low.

Lama ran home and told her dad. He told the village council. A council is a group of people. They are chosen to make decisions for the village. The council met that day. They made a new plan. Each family could take only two buckets of water a day. This kind of plan is called a ration.

The next morning, Lama and her friends helped dig it out. The water inside was still cool and clean. Now the village had two places to find water.

At the end of the week, a truck finally came. It filled the tank. The village was safe again. Everyone learned how a fair ration and some teamwork could help.

versions.title: The Village Without Water
versions.text:
It had not rained in Zahra for many weeks. The ground had turned hard, cracked, and dry. Everyone in the village could feel that something was wrong.

One hot morning, a girl named Lama climbed the hill. She went to check the village's water tank. The tank stores water. Every family depends on it. Lama was shocked. The water level had dropped very low.

Lama hurried home. She told her dad. He quickly told the village council. A council is a group of people. The village chooses them to make important decisions. The council met that afternoon. They agreed on a plan. Each family could take only two buckets of water a day. This would last until the dry spell ended. A plan that limits how much water people may use is called a ration.

That evening, Grandpa remembered something. The younger villagers had forgotten it. Long before the tank was built, the village relied on an old stone cistern. A cistern is a deep pit lined with stone. It collects and stores rain water. It sat behind the old mosque. Years of dust and weeds had hidden it.

The next morning, Lama and her friends worked with the adults. Together, they dug it out. To everyone's relief, the water inside was still cool, clear, and clean. Now the village had two sources of water.

At the end of the week, a large truck finally arrived. It refilled the tank completely. The village was safe again. Everyone learned how a fair ration, an old cistern, and a little teamwork could carry a village through a hard week.

versions.title: The Village Without Water
versions.text:
Imagine waking up to find that your village's water is running out. That is what happened in Zahra during a long, difficult drought.

For many weeks, no rain had fallen. The ground around Zahra had turned hard, cracked, and dry. One hot morning, a girl named Lama climbed the hill to check the main water tank. This tank normally holds enough water for every family. Lama was startled. The water level had dropped close to the bottom.

Lama rushed home to tell her father. He told the village council, a group chosen to make decisions. The council agreed that the village needed to conserve every drop until more water arrived. They created a fair ration. Each family could collect only two buckets of water a day, no matter how much they usually used.

That night, Grandpa remembered an old secret. Long before the tank was built, villagers had relied on a stone cistern hidden behind the old mosque. Over the years, dust and weeds had buried it completely. Most people had forgotten it existed.

The next day, children and adults worked together to cooperate on digging it out. When they reached the bottom, the water inside was still cool, clear, and safe to drink. With two sources of water now available, the scarce supply felt less frightening.

At the end of the week, just as patience was wearing thin, a large truck arrived to resupply the main tank. The village made it through the drought with a fair ration, an old cistern, and neighbors working together.

versions.title: The Village Without Water
versions.text:
Imagine waking up one morning to find that your village's water is quietly running out. That is exactly what happened to Zahra during one of the longest droughts anyone there could remember.

For nearly a month, no rain had fallen. The ground around Zahra had turned hard, cracked, and dry. One scorching morning, a girl named Lama climbed the hill. She went to check the village's main water tank. The tank normally held enough water to supply every family. Lama was startled. The water had dropped close to the very bottom.

Lama rushed home to tell her father. He quickly alerted the village council. A council is a group of respected villagers. They are chosen to make decisions. After a brief discussion, the council agreed on a plan. Everyone needed to conserve every single drop. This would last until more water arrived. They created a fair ration. Each family could collect only two buckets of water per day. This was true no matter how much they normally used.

That same night, Lama's grandfather remembered something important. Younger villagers had forgotten it completely. Long before the tank was built, the people of Zahra relied on a stone cistern. It was hidden behind the old mosque. Over many years, dust and weeds had buried it. Most people no longer remembered it was there.

The next morning, children and adults decided to cooperate. They worked side by side to dig the old cistern free. When they finally reached the bottom, the water inside was still cool, clear, and safe to drink. With two sources of water now available, the village's scarce supply felt far less frightening.

At the end of that long week, patience was wearing thin. Just then, a large truck rumbled in. It came to resupply the main tank with fresh water. The village of Zahra had made it through the drought. A fair ration, a forgotten cistern, and neighbors working together had carried the community through a hard time.

versions.title: The Village Without Water
versions.text:
Imagine waking up one morning to discover that your village's water is quietly running out. That is exactly what happened to Zahra during one of the longest droughts the oldest villagers could remember.

For twenty-six days, not a single drop of rain had fallen. The ground around Zahra had turned hard, cracked, and painfully dry. One scorching morning, a girl named Lama climbed the hill to check the village's main water tank. The tank normally holds about ten thousand liters, enough to supply all forty families for weeks at a time. Lama was startled to find that the water level had dropped close to the very bottom.

Lama rushed home to tell her father. He quickly alerted the village council, a respected group chosen to make important decisions. After a brief but serious discussion, the council agreed that everyone needed to conserve every single drop until more water could arrive. They created a fair ration and posted it on a wooden board in the village square. Each family could collect only two buckets of water per day. This was true no matter how much they normally used at home.

That same night, Lama's grandfather remembered something important that most younger villagers had completely forgotten. Decades before the tank had ever been built, the people of Zahra relied on a stone cistern hidden behind the old mosque. Over many years, drifting dust and tangled weeds had buried the cistern so thoroughly that hardly anyone remembered it still existed.

The next morning, children and adults decided to cooperate, working side by side to dig the old cistern free. When they finally reached the bottom, the rainwater inside was still cool, clear, and perfectly safe to drink. With two separate sources of water now available, the village's scarce supply suddenly felt far less frightening. A few families even shared their extra buckets with elderly neighbors who lived alone.

At the end of that long, anxious week, just as patience had nearly run out, a large truck finally rumbled in to resupply the main tank with several thousand liters of fresh water. The village of Zahra had made it safely through the drought. A fair ration, a forgotten cistern, and neighbors working together had carried the community through a very hard time.

versions.title: The Village Without Water
versions.text:
Few experiences reveal a community's character as clearly as watching its most essential resource disappear. That is precisely what happened in the small village of Zahra during one of the longest droughts its oldest residents could recall.

For twenty-six consecutive days, not a single drop of rain fell. The parched ground around Zahra grew hard, cracked, and increasingly hazardous for crops and animals alike. One scorching morning, a girl named Lama climbed the hill to check the village's main water tank. This reservoir normally holds roughly ten thousand liters, enough to supply all forty families for several weeks. Lama was startled to discover that the water level had dropped to within centimeters of the bottom.

Lama hurried home to alert her father. He immediately informed the village council, a group of respected residents responsible for allocating the community's limited resources. After a brief but urgent discussion, the council concluded that strict conservation was now unavoidable. They devised a fair ration and posted it publicly in the village square. Each family would receive only two buckets of water daily, regardless of their usual consumption, until outside help arrived.

That same evening, Lama's grandfather recalled a detail that most younger villagers had entirely forgotten. Decades before the tank existed, Zahra had depended on a stone cistern concealed behind the old mosque, a structure specifically designed to capture and store seasonal rainwater. Years of drifting dust and tangled weeds had buried it so completely that few people remembered its existence at all.

The following morning, children and adults chose to collaborate rather than work separately. They dug the forgotten cistern free together. When they finally reached its base, they discovered rainwater that remained cool, clear, and entirely safe to drink. With two independent water sources now available, the village's scarcity suddenly felt considerably less threatening. Several families voluntarily shared their extra allowance with elderly neighbors living alone.

By the end of that anxious week, just as communal patience had nearly been exhausted, a large truck finally arrived to resupply the main tank with several thousand liters of fresh water. The ordeal left Zahra with more than a refilled tank. It left the village with a renewed sense of resilience, built on the understanding that a fair ration, a rediscovered cistern, and genuine cooperation could carry an entire community through even its driest week.

versions.title: The Village Without Water
versions.text:
Few experiences reveal a community's underlying character as clearly as watching its most essential resource gradually disappear. That is precisely what unfolded in the small village of Zahra during what its oldest residents described as an unprecedented drought.

For twenty-six consecutive days, not a single drop of rain fell. The parched ground surrounding Zahra grew hard, deeply cracked, and increasingly hazardous for both crops and livestock. One scorching morning, a girl named Lama climbed the hill to inspect the village's main water tank. This reservoir ordinarily holds approximately ten thousand liters, enough to supply all forty families for several consecutive weeks. She was alarmed to discover that the water level had fallen to within mere centimeters of the tank's bottom.

Lama hurried home to alert her father. He immediately informed the village council, a group of respected residents responsible for allocating the community's increasingly limited resources. After a brief yet urgent discussion, the council concluded that strict conservation measures were now unavoidable. They devised a meticulously fair ration and posted it publicly in the village square. Each family would receive precisely two buckets of water daily, regardless of their customary consumption, until outside assistance arrived.

That same evening, Lama's grandfather recalled a detail that most younger villagers had entirely forgotten. Decades before the tank was ever constructed, Zahra had depended upon a stone cistern concealed behind the old mosque, a structure specifically engineered to capture and preserve seasonal rainwater. Years of drifting dust and tangled weeds had buried it so completely that scarcely anyone still remembered its existence.

The following morning, children and adults alike chose to collaborate rather than labor separately. They dug the forgotten cistern free as a unified team. When they finally reached its base, they discovered rainwater that remained remarkably cool, clear, and entirely safe to drink. With two independent water sources now available, the village's scarcity suddenly felt considerably less threatening. Several families voluntarily shared their extra allowance with elderly neighbors living alone.

By the conclusion of that anxious week, just as communal patience had nearly been exhausted, a large truck finally arrived to resupply the main tank with several thousand liters of fresh water. The ordeal left Zahra with far more than a refilled tank. It left the entire village with a renewed sense of resilience, grounded in the understanding that a fair ration, a rediscovered cistern, and genuine collaboration could carry an entire community through even its driest and most uncertain week.

versions.title: The Village Without Water
versions.text:
Few experiences reveal a community's underlying character as unmistakably as watching its most essential resource gradually vanish before everyone's eyes. That is precisely what unfolded in the small village of Zahra during what its oldest residents consistently described as an unprecedented, generation-defining drought.

For twenty-six consecutive days, not a single drop of rain fell. The parched earth surrounding Zahra grew hard, deeply fissured, and increasingly hazardous for both crops and livestock alike. One scorching morning, a girl named Lama climbed the hill to inspect the village's main water tank. This reservoir ordinarily holds approximately ten thousand liters, sufficient to supply all forty families for several consecutive weeks under normal conditions. She was alarmed to discover that the water level had fallen to within mere centimeters of the tank's bottom.

Lama hurried home to alert her father. He immediately informed the village council, a group of respected residents entrusted with allocating the community's increasingly limited resources fairly. After a brief yet urgent deliberation, the council concluded that strict conservation measures had become not merely advisable but unavoidable. They devised a meticulously fair ration and posted it publicly in the village square. Each family would receive precisely two buckets of water daily, regardless of customary consumption, until outside assistance eventually arrived.

That same evening, Lama's grandfather recalled a detail that most younger villagers had entirely forgotten with the passing of time. Decades before the tank was ever constructed, Zahra had depended upon a stone cistern concealed behind the old mosque, a structure specifically engineered by earlier generations to capture and preserve seasonal rainwater for exactly such emergencies. Years of drifting dust and tangled weeds had buried it so thoroughly that scarcely anyone still remembered its existence at all.

The following morning, children and adults alike chose to collaborate rather than labor separately, excavating the forgotten cistern free as a single, unified team working from dawn until dusk. When they finally reached its base, they discovered rainwater that remained remarkably cool, clear, and entirely safe to drink. With two independent sources now available, the village's scarcity suddenly felt considerably less threatening, and several families voluntarily shared their extra allowance with elderly neighbors who lived alone and could not collect water themselves.

By the conclusion of that anxious week, just as communal patience had nearly been exhausted entirely, a large truck finally arrived to resupply the main tank with several thousand additional liters of fresh water. The ordeal left Zahra with far more than merely a refilled tank. It left the entire village with a renewed and lasting sense of resilience, grounded firmly in the understanding that a fair ration, a rediscovered cistern, and genuine collaboration could carry an entire community through even its driest and most uncertain week of the year.

versions.title: The Village Without Water
versions.text:
The small village of Zahra endured, during one scorching season, what its oldest residents would later describe as the most severe drought within living memory, a twenty-six-day stretch without a single drop of rain that left the surrounding earth hard, deeply fissured, and increasingly hazardous for crops and livestock alike. It was during this crisis that a girl named Lama climbed the hill one scorching morning to inspect the village's main water tank, an ordinarily reliable reservoir holding roughly ten thousand liters, enough to supply all forty families for several consecutive weeks, only to discover that its level had fallen to within mere centimeters of the bottom.

Lama's discovery set in motion a rapid and disciplined response. Her father alerted the village council, a group of respected residents responsible for allocating the community's increasingly scarce resources, and the council concluded within hours that strict conservation had become unavoidable. They devised a meticulously fair ration, publicly posted in the village square, under which each family would receive precisely two buckets of water daily regardless of customary consumption, a limit intended to stretch the dwindling supply until outside assistance could arrive.

That same evening, a piece of nearly forgotten village history proved unexpectedly useful. Lama's grandfather recalled that decades before the tank had ever been constructed, Zahra had depended upon a stone cistern concealed behind the old mosque, a structure earlier generations had engineered specifically to capture and preserve seasonal rainwater for emergencies exactly like this one, though years of drifting dust and tangled weeds had buried it so thoroughly that scarcely anyone still remembered its existence.

The following morning, children and adults set aside any division of labor and chose instead to collaborate as a single team, excavating the forgotten cistern until they reached its base, where they found rainwater that remained remarkably cool, clear, and entirely safe to drink. With two independent sources of water now available, the village's scarcity suddenly felt far less threatening, and several families went so far as to voluntarily share their own limited allowance with elderly neighbors who lived alone and could not collect water for themselves.

By the time a large truck finally arrived at the end of that anxious week to resupply the main tank with several thousand additional liters, the people of Zahra had gained something more lasting than a refilled reservoir: a renewed sense of resilience, built on the shared understanding that a fair ration, a rediscovered cistern, and genuine collaboration between neighbors could carry an entire community through even its driest and most uncertain week.

versions.title: The Village Without Water
versions.text:
The small village of Zahra endured, during one unforgiving season, what its oldest residents would later describe as the most severe drought within living memory, a twenty-six-day stretch without a single drop of rain that left the surrounding earth hard, deeply fissured, and increasingly hazardous for crops and livestock alike. Lama's unsettling discovery set in motion a rapid and remarkably disciplined response. Her father immediately alerted the village council, a group of respected residents entrusted with allocating the community's increasingly scarce resources fairly, and the council concluded within hours that strict conservation measures had become not merely prudent but entirely unavoidable. They devised a meticulously fair ration, publicly posted in the village square, under which each family would receive precisely two buckets of water daily regardless of customary consumption, a deliberate limit intended to stretch the rapidly dwindling supply until outside assistance could eventually arrive.

That same evening, a piece of nearly forgotten village history proved unexpectedly indispensable. Lama's grandfather recalled that decades before the tank had ever been constructed, Zahra had depended entirely upon a stone cistern concealed behind the old mosque, a structure that earlier generations had deliberately engineered to capture and preserve seasonal rainwater for emergencies exactly like this one, though years of drifting dust and tangled weeds had buried it so thoroughly that scarcely anyone still remembered its existence at all.

The following morning, children and adults alike set aside any customary division of labor and chose instead to collaborate as a single, unified team, excavating the long-forgotten cistern until they finally reached its base, where they discovered rainwater that remained remarkably cool, clear, and entirely safe to drink. With two independent sources of water now available, the village's underlying scarcity suddenly felt considerably less threatening, and several families went so far as to voluntarily share their own limited allowance with elderly neighbors who lived alone and could not collect water for themselves.

By the time a large truck finally arrived at the end of that anxious week to resupply the main tank with several thousand additional liters, the people of Zahra had gained something considerably more lasting than a merely refilled reservoir: a deeply renewed sense of resilience, grounded in the shared understanding that a fair ration, a rediscovered cistern, and genuine collaboration between neighbors could carry an entire community through even its driest, most uncertain, and most demanding week of the year.

questions.stem: Why did the village council create a ration?

wrong.A: The ration was not a punishment for anyone.
wrong.C: The article does not mention buying water.
wrong.D: The ration was meant to help, not to test people.

questions.stem: In the article, the word scarce means —

completely gone forever with none left at all
stored safely underground for later use by people
very hard to find because there is little of it
questions.why: After the drought began, water became scarce, meaning there was only a little of it and it was hard to get.

wrong.A: Scarce means the opposite of easy to find.
wrong.B: The village still had some water, just very little.
wrong.C: Scarce describes an amount, not a storage place.

wrong.B: His memory directly helped solve the problem.
wrong.D: The cistern was built long ago, not that week.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe both the ration and the cistern in detail?
options: To explain exactly how to build a new mosque in the village
To compare the village of Zahra with a much larger city

To show two ways the village coped with a serious water shortage

wrong.A: The article is not a building guide for mosques.
wrong.B: The article never compares Zahra to a city.
wrong.C: The truck was still needed to resupply the tank.

MID.prompt: Explain how the village council's ration and Lama's grandfather's memory of the cistern worked together to help the village. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained how the ration and the cistern worked together.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The council's ration and the old cistern worked as a team to save the village. First, the council limited each family to two buckets a day, which made the tank's remaining water last longer. Then, Lama's grandfather remembered the old cistern behind the mosque, and the children and adults cooperated to dig it out, giving the village a second source of clean water. Together, these two solutions kept Zahra safe until the truck finally arrived to resupply the tank.

keyWords.definition: the careful use and protection of a limited resource
keyWords.example: The city launched a water conservation program during the dry summer.

keyWords.definition: to give out a limited amount of something according to a plan
keyWords.example: The teacher allocated ten minutes to each group for their presentation.

keyWords.definition: a situation in which something needed is in short or limited supply
keyWords.example: The scarcity of fresh vegetables made prices rise sharply that winter.

keyWords.definition: to work closely with other people to achieve a shared result
keyWords.example: Scientists from three countries collaborated on the new vaccine.

keyWords.definition: the ability to recover well from a difficult or damaging situation
keyWords.example: The town's resilience after the storm impressed the visiting reporters.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the article?

A village abandons its old mosque during a very difficult drought, then moves away

wrong.C: The whole community, not one family, solved the problem.
wrong.D: The existing tank was refilled, not rebuilt.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article by emphasizing the village's 'resilience' rather than simply saying the tank was refilled?

wrong.B: The council's decisions are presented positively throughout.
wrong.C: The truck's resupply was an essential part of the solution.

HIGH.prompt: The poll suggests that one person's small effort cannot make a real difference during a big problem like a drought. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the article about the ration, the cistern, and the village's collaboration.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree with the poll statement. In the article, Lama's single decision to check the tank started the entire chain of solutions that saved the village, and her grandfather's one memory of the forgotten cistern provided an entire second water source. Someone might argue that the council's ration and the water truck's resupply mattered more than any individual, since they affected the whole village at once. However, those larger solutions only existed because individuals first noticed the problem, allocated resources fairly, and chose to collaborate, which shows that small, individual actions can set much larger solutions into motion.
